catalog_quote: Khan & Weise 2013: 238: "Stress\nAs in Standard German (Kohler 1999: 87), stress in native roots can be considered primarily initial or penultimate (see Wiese 1996: Section 8), while borrowed and polymorphemic words can exhibit other stress patterns. Because of this potential for ambiguity, stress is transcribed in all polysyllabic examples in this entry. For a detailed account of how stress interacts with intonation in other varieties of Upper Saxon, see Kügler (2005, 2007) for the Leipzig dialect and Selting (2002a, b), Peters (2004), and Gilles (2005) for the Dresden dialect." — Franke 1884: 36, §65: "In allen german. Sprachen trägt die Stammsilbe den Wortaccent. Infolge davon verkümmerten Ende der ahd. Zeit die Vokale der Bildungssilben zu e oder <e" [scan '<e' = æ] — Goepfert 1878: 63: "Die Betonung der Composita anlangend, liegt wie im Nhd. der Hauptton stets auf dem ersten, der Nebenton auf dem zweiten Theile; eine Ausnahme machen auch hier die mit untrennbarer Partikel zusammengesetzten Worte." — Goepfert 1878: 20: "... legte man den Hauptton in solcher Stärke auf die Stammsilbe, dass für [scan 'ftir'] die Endungen oft kaum noch ein Rest von Betonung blieb."

new_statements.translation: Franke: 'In all Germanic languages the stem syllable carries the word accent. As a result, at the end of the OHG period the vowels of the formative syllables were reduced to e or æ.' Goepfert: 'As regards the accentuation of compounds, as in NHG the main stress always lies on the first part, the secondary stress on the second; here too words compounded with an inseparable particle are an exception.'

Because of this potential for ambiguity, stress is transcribed in all polysyllabic examples in this entry.' followed by the Kuegler/Selting/Peters/Gilles p…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress works as in Standard German: native words stress the root/stem syllable, which in mono- and disyllabic native roots surfaces as initial (or penultimate) stress; unstressed prefixes (be-, ge-, ver- etc.) and inflectional/derivational endings are unstressed and heavily reduced; loanwords and polymorphemic words may carry stress elsewhere (Leipzig speech even retracts stress to the first syllable in some loans, Albrecht 1881 §149); compounds take main stress on the first member, secondary on the second, inseparable-prefix formations excepted.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Goepfert 1878: 63 — in compounds the Nebenton falls on the second member. Khan & Weise say nothing about secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Borrowed and polymorphemic words can have other patterns (Khan & Weise); inseparable-prefix words do not take initial main stress (Goepfert); Leipzig dialect shifts stress to the first syllable in loans like Bureau, Bazar, Cacao, Papa and to the ending in -ik/-iker words (Albrecht 1881 §149).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress; Khan & Weise mark stress on every polysyllabic word in citation forms and in the connected North Wind passage. Franke §7 separately describes the characteristic two-peaked rising-falling syllable/word pitch contour of Meissnisch ('singing' accent), which concerns tonal realisation, not stress position.
new_statements.identity_note: Khan & Weise 2013 describe the urban Chemnitz variety (Vorerzgebirgisch), which they and Bergmann 1990 place as transitional between Meissnisch, Vogtländisch and Erzgebirgisch but treat as Upper Saxon; it falls under uppe1400. Franke 1884 covers Meissnisch/Osterländisch/Dessau-Herzberg Upper Saxon proper (core uppe1400). Goepfert 1878 is West Erzgebirgisch (Annaberg/Marienberg), an Upper Saxon–East Franconian transition zone, so it is supporting evidence only. Glottolog's uppe1400 'Central East Middle German' also subsumes Thuringian and some Silesian/Transylvanian refs; the statement quoted is for Upper Saxon.

sources.note: §149 'Verschiebung des Tones' (pp. 28-29): loanwords such as Bureau, Bazar, Cacao, Papa, Mama get stress on the first syllable in Leipzig speech; words in -ik/-iker stress the ending; no general statement of the native stress rule (taken for granted as Standard German).

sources.citation: Franke, Carl G. 1884. Der obersächsische Dialekt. Abhandlung zum Programm der Realschule II. Ordnung zu Leisnig (Progr. Nr. 518). Leipzig: Breitkopf & Härtel. 56 pp.
sources.note: §65 p. 36: 'In allen german. Sprachen trägt die Stammsilbe den Wortaccent' (stem syllable bears word accent), used to explain reduction of formative syllables; §7 pp. 9-10 describes the two-peaked rising-falling syllable accent of Meissnisch/Osterländisch vs. one-peaked accent of Dessau-Herzberg and differences in word/sentence accent contour (e.g. Grossenhain, dahin), i.e. pitch contour, not stress placement.

sources.citation: Goepfert, Ernst. 1878. Die Mundart des sächsischen Erzgebirges nach den Lautverhältnissen, der Wortbildung und Flexion. Leipzig: Veit & Comp.
sources.note: pp. 20-21: reduction of inflectional/derivational syllables explained by the word accent settling on the root syllables ('legte man den Hauptton in solcher Stärke auf die Stammsilbe'); p. 63: in compounds the Hauptton lies, as in NHG, always on the first member, Nebenton on the second, except words with inseparable particles. West Erzgebirgisch (transitional variety).
